In the mathematical field of [[differential geometry]], a '''biharmonic map''' is a map between [[Riemannian manifold|Riemannian]] or [[pseudo-Riemannian manifold]]s which satisfies a certain fourth-order [[partial differential equation]]. A '''biharmonic submanifold''' refers to an embedding or immersion into a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold which is a biharmonic map when the domain is equipped with its induced metric. The problem of understanding biharmonic maps was posed by [[James Eells]] and Luc Lemaire in 1983.{{sfnm|1a1=Eells|1a2=Lemaire|1y=1983|1loc=(8.7) and (8.8)}} The study of [[harmonic map]]s, of which the study of biharmonic maps is an outgrowth (any harmonic map is also a biharmonic map), had been (and remains) an active field of study for the previous twenty years.{{sfnm|1a1=Eells|1a2=Sampson|1y=1964}} A simple case of biharmonic maps is given by [[biharmonic equation|biharmonic functions]].

==Definition==
Given Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifolds {{math|(''M'', ''g'')}} and {{math|(''N'', ''h'')}}, a map {{mvar|f}} from {{mvar|M}} to {{mvar|N}} which is differentiable at least four times is called a ''biharmonic map'' if
<math display="block">\Delta\Delta f+\sum_{i=1}^m R^h\big(\Delta f,df(e_i),df(e_i)\big)=0;</math>
given any point {{mvar|p}} of {{mvar|M}}, each side of this equation is an element of the [[tangent space]] to {{mvar|N}} at {{math|''f''(''p'')}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Jiang|1y=1986|1loc=Definition 5|2a1=Chen|2y=2011|2loc=eq. (7.64)}} In other words, the above equation is an equality of sections of the [[vector bundle]] {{math|''f''<sup> *</sup>''TN'' → ''M''}}. In the equation, {{math|''e''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''e''<sub>''m''</sub>}} is an arbitrary {{mvar|g}}-orthonormal basis of the [[tangent space]] to {{mvar|M}} and {{math|''R''<sup>''h''</sup>}} is the [[Riemann curvature tensor]], following the convention {{math|1=''R''(''u'', ''v'', ''w'') = ∇<sub>''u''</sub>∇<sub>''v''</sub>''w'' − ∇<sub>''v''</sub>∇<sub>''u''</sub>''w'' − ∇<sub>[''u'', ''v'']</sub>w}}. The quantity {{math|∆''f''}} is the "tension field" or "Laplacian" of {{mvar|f}}, as was introduced by Eells and Sampson in the study of harmonic maps.{{sfnm|1a1=Eells|1a2=Sampson|1y=1964|1p=116}}

In terms of the [[Trace (linear algebra)|trace]], [[interior product]], and [[Pullback (differential geometry)|pullback]] operations, the biharmonic map equation can be written as
<math display="block">\Delta\Delta f+\operatorname{tr}_g\Big(f^\ast\big(\iota_{\Delta f}R^h\big)\Big)=0.</math>
In terms of local coordinates {{math|''x''<sup>''i''</sup>}} for {{mvar|M}} and local coordinates {{math|''y''<sup>α</sup>}} for {{mvar|N}}, the biharmonic map equation is written as
<math display="block">g^{ij} \left(
    \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} \left(\frac{\partial(\Delta f)^\alpha}{\partial x^j}+\frac{\partial f^\beta}{\partial x^j}\Gamma_{\beta\gamma}^\alpha(\Delta f)^\gamma\right)
    -
    \Gamma_{ij}^k \left(\frac{\partial(\Delta f)^\alpha}{\partial x^k}+\frac{\partial f^\beta}{\partial x^k}\Gamma_{\beta\gamma}^\alpha(\Delta f)^\gamma\right)
    +
    \frac{\partial f^\delta}{\partial x^i} \Gamma_{\delta\epsilon}^\alpha\left(\frac{\partial(\Delta f)^\epsilon}{\partial x^j}+\frac{\partial f^\beta}{\partial x^j}\Gamma_{\beta\gamma}^\epsilon(\Delta f)^\gamma\right)
\right)
+ g^{ij} R_{\beta\gamma\delta}^\alpha (\Delta f)^\beta\frac{\partial f^\gamma}{\partial x^i}\frac{\partial f^\delta}{\partial x^j}
= 0,</math>
in which the [[Einstein summation convention]] is used with the following definitions of the [[Christoffel symbols]], [[Riemann curvature tensor]], and [[harmonic map|tension field]]:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\Gamma_{ij}^k &= \frac{1}{2}g^{kl}\left(\frac{\partial g_{jl}}{\partial x^i}+\frac{\partial g_{il}}{\partial x^j}-\frac{\partial g_{ij}}{\partial x^l}\right) \\
\Gamma_{\beta\gamma}^\alpha &= \frac{1}{2}h^{\alpha\delta} \left(\frac{\partial h_{\gamma\delta}}{\partial y^\beta}+\frac{\partial h_{\beta\delta}}{\partial y^\gamma} - \frac{\partial h_{\beta\gamma}}{\partial y^\delta}\right) \\
R_{\beta\gamma\delta}^\alpha &= \frac{\partial\Gamma_{\gamma\delta}^\alpha}{\partial y^\beta}-\frac{\partial\Gamma_{\beta\delta}^\alpha}{\partial y^\gamma}+\Gamma_{\beta\rho}^\alpha\Gamma_{\gamma\delta}^\rho-\Gamma_{\gamma\rho}^\alpha\Gamma_{\beta\delta}^\rho\\
\left(\Delta f\right)^\alpha &= g^{ij} \left(\frac{\partial^2f^\alpha}{\partial x^i\partial x^j}-\Gamma_{ij}^k\frac{\partial f^\alpha}{\partial x^k}+\frac{\partial f^\beta}{\partial x^i}\Gamma_{\beta\gamma}^\alpha\frac{\partial f^\gamma}{\partial x^j}\right).
\end{align}</math>
It is clear from any of these presentations of the equation that any harmonic map is automatically biharmonic. For this reason, a ''proper biharmonic map'' refers to a biharmonic map which is not harmonic.

In the special setting where {{mvar|f}} is a (pseudo-)Riemannian immersion, meaning that it is an [[Immersion (mathematics)|immersion]] and that {{mvar|g}} is equal to the [[induced metric]] {{math|''f''<sup> *</sup>''h''}}, one says that one has a ''biharmonic submanifold'' instead of a biharmonic map. Since the [[mean curvature|mean curvature vector]] of {{mvar|f}} is equal to the laplacian of {{math|''f'' : (''M'', ''f''<sup> *</sup>''h'') → (''N'', ''h'')}}, one knows that an immersion is [[minimal submanifold|minimal]] if and only if it is harmonic. In particular, any minimal immersion is automatically a biharmonic [[submanifold]]. A ''proper biharmonic submanifold'' refers to a biharmonic submanifold which is not minimal.

The motivation for the biharmonic map equation is from the ''bienergy functional''
<math display="block">E_2(f) = \frac{1}{2} \, \int_M \left|\Delta f\right|_h^2 \, dv_g,</math>
in the setting where {{mvar|M}} is [[closed manifold|closed]] and {{mvar|g}} and {{mvar|h}} are both Riemannian; {{math|''dv''<sub>''g''</sub>}} denotes the volume [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] on <math>M</math> induced by {{mvar|g}}. Eells & Lemaire, in 1983, suggested the study of [[Critical point (mathematics)|critical points]] of this functional.{{sfnm|1a1=Eells|1a2=Lemaire|1y=1983|1loc=(8.7)}} Guo Ying Jiang, in 1986, calculated its first variation formula, thereby finding the above biharmonic map equation as the corresponding [[Euler–Lagrange equation|Euler-Lagrange equation]].{{sfnm|1a1=Jiang|1y=1986|1loc=Theorem 3}} Harmonic maps correspond to critical points for which the bioenergy functional takes on its minimal possible value of zero.

==Examples and classification==
A number of examples of biharmonic maps, such as inverses of [[stereographic projection]]s in the special case of four dimensions, and inversions of punctured [[Euclidean space]], are known.{{sfnm|1a1=Montaldo|1a2=Oniciuc|1y=2006|1loc=Sections 5−7}} There are many examples of biharmonic submanifolds, such as (for any {{mvar|k}}) the generalized [[Clifford torus]]
<math display="block">\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n+2}:x_1^2+\cdots+x_{k+1}^2=x_{k+2}^2+\cdots+x_{n+2}^2 = \frac{1}{2}\right\},</math>
as a submanifold of the {{math|(''n'' + 1)}}-sphere.{{sfnm|1a1=Jiang|1y=1986|1loc=Example 12}} It is minimal if and only if {{mvar|n}} is even and equal to {{math|2''k''}}.

The biharmonic curves in three-dimensional [[space form]]s can be studied via the [[Frenet equations]]. It follows easily that every constant-speed biharmonic curve in a three-dimensional space form of nonpositive curvature must be geodesic.{{sfnm|1a1=Caddeo|1a2=Montaldo|1a3=Oniciuc|1y=2001|1loc=Proposition 3.1}} Any constant-speed biharmonic curves in the round three-dimensional sphere {{math|''S''<sup>3</sup>}} can be viewed as the solution of a certain [[Linear_differential_equation#Homogeneous_equation_with_constant_coefficients|constant-coefficient fourth-order linear ordinary differential equation]] for a {{math|'''R'''<sup>4</sup>}}-valued function.{{sfnm|1a1=Caddeo|1a2=Montaldo|1a3=Oniciuc|1y=2001|1loc=Proposition 3.2}} As such the situation can be completely analyzed, with the result that any such curve is, up to an isometry of the sphere:
* a constant-speed parametrization of the intersection of {{math|''S''<sup>3</sup> ⊂ '''R'''<sup>4</sup>}} with the two-dimensional linear subspace {{math|'''R''' × '''R''' × {0} × {0}<nowiki/>}}
* a constant-speed parametrization of the intersection of {{math|''S''<sup>3</sup> ⊂ '''R'''<sup>4</sup>}} with the two-dimensional affine subspace {{math|'''R''' × '''R''' × {''d''<sub>1</sub>} × {''d''<sub>2</sub>}<nowiki/>}}, for any choice of {{math|(''d''<sub>1</sub>, ''d''<sub>2</sub>)}} which is on the circle of radius {{math|2<sup>−1/2</sup>}} around the origin in {{math|'''R'''<sup>2</sup>}}
* a constant-speed reparametrization of <math display="block">t\mapsto \Big(\frac{\cos at}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{\sin at}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{\cos bt}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{\sin bt}{\sqrt{2}}\Big)</math> for any {{math|(''a'', ''b'')}} on the circle of radius {{math|2<sup>1/2</sup>}} around the origin in {{math|'''R'''<sup>2</sup>}}.
In particular, every constant-speed biharmonic curve in {{math|''S''<sup>3</sup>}} has constant [[geodesic curvature]].

As a consequence of the purely local study of the [[Gauss-Codazzi equations]] and the biharmonic map equation, any connected biharmonic surface in {{math|''S''<sup>3</sup>}} must have constant mean curvature.{{sfnm|1a1=Caddeo|1a2=Montaldo|1a3=Oniciuc|1y=2001|1loc=Theorem 4.5}} If it is nonzero (so that the surface is not minimal) then the [[second fundamental form]] must have constant length equal to {{math|2<sup>1/2</sup>}}, as follows from the biharmonic map equation. Surfaces with such strong geometric conditions can be completely classified, with the result that any connected biharmonic surface in {{math|''S''<sup>3</sup>}} must be either locally (up to isometry) part of the hypersphere
<math display="block">\left\{\Big((w,x,y,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\Big):w^2+x^2+y^2=\frac{1}{2}\right\},</math>
or minimal.{{sfnm|1a1=Caddeo|1a2=Montaldo|1a3=Oniciuc|1y=2001|1loc=Theorem 4.8}} In a similar way, any biharmonic hypersurface of [[Euclidean space]] which has constant mean curvature must be minimal.{{sfnm|1a1=Chen|1y=2011|1loc=Corollary 2.10}}

Guo Ying Jiang showed that if {{mvar|g}} and {{mvar|h}} are Riemannian, and if {{mvar|M}} is closed and {{mvar|h}} has nonpositive [[sectional curvature]], then a map from {{math|(''M'', ''g'')}} to {{math|(''N'', ''h'')}} is biharmonic if and only if it is harmonic.{{sfnm|1a1=Jiang|1y=1986|1loc=Proposition 7}} The proof is to show that, due to the sectional curvature assumption, the Laplacian of {{math|{{!}}∆''f''{{!}}<sup>2</sup>}} is nonnegative, at which point the [[maximum principle]] applies. This result and proof can be compared to Eells & Sampson's vanishing theorem, which says that if additionally the [[Ricci curvature]] of {{mvar|g}} is nonnegative, then a map from {{math|(''M'', ''g'')}} to {{math|(''N'', ''h'')}} is harmonic if and only if it is [[totally geodesic]].{{sfnm|1a1=Eells|1a2=Sampson|1y=1964|1p=124}} As a special case of Jiang's result, a closed submanifold of a Riemannian manifold of nonpositive sectional curvature is biharmonic if and only if it is minimal. Partly based on these results, it was conjectured by R. Caddeo, [[Stefano Montaldo|S. Montaldo]] and C. Oniciuc that ''every'' biharmonic submanifold of a Riemannian manifold of nonpositive sectional curvature must be minimal.{{sfnm|1a1=Caddeo|1a2=Montaldo|1a3=Oniciuc|1y=2001|1p=869}} This, however, is now known to be false.{{sfnm|1a1=Chen|1y=2011|1p=147}} The special case of submanifolds of Euclidean space is an older conjecture of [[Bang-Yen Chen]].{{sfnm|1a1=Chen|1y=1991|1loc=Conjecture 3|2a1=Chen|2y=1996|2loc=Conjecture 25.B.6}} Chen's conjecture has been proven in a number of geometrically special cases.{{sfnm|1a1=Chen|1y=1996|1loc=Theorems 15.4, 15.6−15.8, 15.10, 15.12−15.13}}
